Droz Farny Circles

GeometryTrianglesCircles
Game: Move a point in a triangle to see two circles built from the feet of its perpendiculars, and check whether they stay the same size.
How to play: Drag P or a corner, or focus a dot and use the arrow keys. Tick the Show boxes to draw the circles, then press Reset to start again.
Look for the math

Pick any point P in a triangle and find its mirror partner Q across the angle bisectors. Drop perpendiculars from P to the three side lines. Circles drawn from those feet through Q cut the side lines in six points. Surprisingly, all six lie on one circle centred at P, and doing the same with Q gives a circle of exactly the same size.

Finding the partner Q

At corner A the applet measures the angle between AB and AP, then turns the other side AC by that same angle. The line it lands on is the mirror image of AP in the angle bisector; the applet does the same at B and C and crosses the lines from A and B to find Q. That Q is the isogonal conjugate of P. The logic test compares the crossing with the barycentric formula Q = (a²/α : b²/β : c²/γ) on hundreds of triangles and gets the same point every time. This page is a different theorem from its sibling Droz-Farny: that one puts two perpendicular lines through the orthocenter and asks about collinear midpoints. Here the claim is about two congruent circles.

Six points, one circle

Each pedal circle foot Pa is the closest point of the side BC to P. The circle centred at Pa passing through Q meets the line BC in two points, say Y and Y′. Because PaQ = PaY, the perpendicular at Pa and the side line make a right triangle, so PY² = PPa² + PaY² = PPa² + PaQ². The same calculation at Pb, Pc gives the same distance from P: the six cut points lie on one circle centred at P. The test measured all six distances in over 3,000 configurations; they agreed with the drawn radius to better than a millionth of the picture's size. Tick circles P and radii to see the six points and the circle.

Why the two radii agree

Let M be the midpoint of PQ. The median formula in triangle PaPQ turns the last expression into the page's claim

PY² = 2·PaM² + PQ²/2

Here PaM is the radius of the pedal circle of P, which does not depend on which side was chosen. The pedal circles of P and Q are the same circle (the test checked all six feet lie equally far from M), so swapping P and Q leaves PaM unchanged. Hence both large circles have the same radius R = √(2ρ² + PQ²/2), where ρ is that common pedal radius. The test checked the formula and the equality of the two reconstructed radii in every well-conditioned configuration, and checked the page's special case P = O, Q = H (circumcenter and orthocenter) in 120 triangles.

What the applet actually draws

The applet rebuilds each large circle from only the first cut point on each side: it takes their circumcenter and the average of the three distances to it. That comes back to P (or Q) and to the radius R whenever the three points are spread out; when they almost line up, the reconstruction is numerically fragile, and the test leaves those few cases to the direct six-point check. If P comes within 2 pixels of the circumcircle, the applet stops drawing Q at all; this page does the same. The Reset button and the keyboard shortcut R are additions to the applet's six Show checkboxes.

Tick both circles P and circles Q and drag P slowly: the two green and purple circles slide around but keep one radius. Then drag P onto the circle through A, B and C and watch Q disappear.
